bp: The ordinary problem is a public claim that arrives as words plus an image: a caption, screenshot, meme, news photo, chart, or social post. People share these mixed claims more effectively than plain text claims, so a fact-checking system has to decide whether the whole package is supported by evidence. The hard part is that the truth may sit in the relation between the words and the picture, not in either one alone. A real checker may need to ask whether the image is actually about the described event, whether the text changes the meaning of the image, and whether outside evidence agrees. This paper serves that setting by building FACTCOMPASS, a system for multimodal fact-checking. It combines a model that can read both pictures and text with retrieval, meaning it brings in outside evidence, and with reasoning training, meaning it teaches the model to explain and check its steps instead of giving only a label.
wh: The difficulty starts because visual evidence is not just another sentence. An image can contain objects, places, dates, signs, layouts, and implied context, but those details may be only loosely connected to the claim. Existing multimodal large language model methods, according to the abstract, do not fully use visual evidence. That means they may look at the image but fail to ask which visible parts matter for the factual question. The second difficulty is explanation. Rigid fine-tuning templates can train a model to produce a fixed style of answer, but fact-checking needs context-aware reasoning: different claims require different evidence paths. Some claims need matching a photo to an event; some need checking background knowledge; some need comparing text against retrieved records. If the model follows a fixed answer pattern, it can sound orderly while missing the actual reason a claim is true or false.
naive: A smart beginner might take a strong multimodal model, give it the claim and the attached image, and ask it to decide true or false with a short explanation. If that is not enough, they might fine-tune it on fact-checking examples using a standard prompt template. This fails in two ways described by the paper. First, the model may not bring in the right outside evidence, especially relevant images or knowledge-level text evidence. Second, a fixed template can reward answers that have the right shape rather than the right reasoning. The system may learn to imitate fact-checking language without deeply comparing the claim, the image, and external evidence.
ap: The core move is to turn fact-checking from a one-shot judgment into a guided evidence-and-reasoning process. FACTCOMPASS adds a retrieval module that searches for semantically relevant evidence images, enriches understanding of the claim-related image, and refines textual evidence using knowledge. In plain terms, it tries to gather better things to look at before asking the model to judge. Then it trains the model's reasoning in stages. It first uses GPT-4o reasoning on part of the fact-checking data as a cold start, so the model sees examples of step-by-step checking. It then broadens reasoning with prior knowledge and rejection sampling, keeping candidate reasoning paths that pass a rule-based filter. Finally, it uses Group Relative Policy Optimization to compare multiple reasoning paths and push the model toward paths that are more factually consistent.
mech: The mechanism begins with a multimodal claim: text plus a related image. FACTCOMPASS does not treat this pair as complete evidence. It sends the claim and image into a retrieval stage. That stage looks for evidence images that are close in meaning to the claim and original image, adds context around the claim-related image, and refines the text evidence at a knowledge level. The output of this stage is a richer evidence bundle: the original claim, the original image, retrieved visual material, and sharpened textual evidence. The model then uses this bundle to reason about the claim. Training happens in a self-refining sequence. First, reasoning traces from GPT-4o are distilled from partially fact-checking data, giving the system initial examples of how a checker might connect evidence to a conclusion. Next, broader data are used to activate more reasoning paths, with prior knowledge guiding what to try and rejection sampling throwing away poor candidates. Rejection sampling here means generating possible explanations and keeping only those that satisfy rule-based requirements. Last, Group Relative Policy Optimization compares groups of candidate reasoning paths rather than judging each path alone. Paths that better preserve factual consistency receive stronger training signal, so the model learns not just to answer, but to prefer evidence-grounded explanations.
math: Several mathematical ideas sit underneath the paper. The first is similarity: the retrieval module needs a way to decide which outside images or pieces of text are meaningfully close to the claim. Similarity compresses many details into a score, so the system must choose which differences matter, such as objects, scene meaning, or claim topic, and which can be ignored. The second idea is ranking, because retrieval is not only finding evidence but ordering possible evidence so the most useful items are seen first. The third idea is learning from examples: GPT-4o reasoning traces become demonstrations, and the model adjusts its behavior to imitate useful checking steps. The fourth is reinforcement learning, explained plainly as repeated trial and feedback. The model tries reasoning paths; rules and factual-consistency checks decide which paths are better; training pushes future answers toward the better ones. Group Relative Policy Optimization adds comparison within a group, so quality is judged relatively among several possible chains. The tradeoff is accuracy versus control: rules can encourage consistency, but they can only reward what they are able to detect.
dots: This paper connects three recurring conference ideas. From retrieval and search, it takes the view that a model should not answer from the claim alone when outside evidence can be fetched. From multimodal vision-language work, it treats images and text as different evidence sources that must be aligned, not merely placed side by side. From reinforcement learning for language models, it uses feedback to shape the kind of reasoning the model prefers. It also sits near misinformation and trust research, where the central question is not only whether a system can classify a post, but whether it can justify the decision with evidence that a human checker could inspect. Neighboring papers on ranking, retrieval-augmented generation, and model reasoning face the same deeper pressure: a fluent model can produce an answer before it has gathered or compared enough evidence. FACTCOMPASS is one answer to that pressure in the specific setting of text-image claims.
ww: The approach should help because it attacks the two failures named in the abstract separately. Better retrieval gives the model more relevant things to compare. If the original image is misleading, reused, or incomplete, retrieved evidence images and refined text evidence can provide missing context. That changes the task from guessing from a single post to comparing a claim against a small evidence set. The staged reasoning training then changes how the model uses that evidence. Distilled reasoning gives it an initial pattern for explaining a fact-check. Prior knowledge and rejection sampling widen the set of possible reasoning paths while filtering out weak ones. Group-relative training makes the model choose among alternatives, which is useful because fact-checking often has several plausible stories but only some remain consistent with the evidence. In plain terms, the system works by making the model look in more places, then rewarding the explanations that keep the claim, images, and knowledge aligned.
po: The payoff is a multimodal fact-checking system that should make fuller use of visual evidence and produce deeper, more context-aware explanations than rigid template-based fine-tuning. The abstract claims extensive experiments show the effectiveness of FACTCOMPASS. The concrete capability is not merely labeling a mixed text-image claim, but improving evidence utilization: retrieving relevant evidence images, enriching the context around the claim image, refining text evidence, and training reasoning paths toward factual consistency. For misinformation settings, that matters because a user or moderator needs to know why the image-and-text package is misleading or supported, not only receive a bare verdict.
limits: The abstract does not state the datasets, metrics, baselines, languages, claim types, or failure cases, so the strength of the evidence cannot be judged from this record alone. The system assumes the retrieval module can find semantically relevant evidence images and useful knowledge-level text evidence; if the needed evidence is absent, mislabeled, manipulated, or ranked poorly, later reasoning may still fail. It also assumes rule-based reinforcement signals can capture factual consistency well enough to guide learning. Rules can miss subtle visual deception or reward explanations that satisfy surface checks. Distilling GPT-4o reasoning may transfer useful patterns, but it can also transfer teacher mistakes or styles not suited to every fact-checking domain.
